en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 9.
Campeyyakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Campā)
1. The Story of the Monk of the Kassapa Clan At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond.
Now at that time, in the country of Kāsī, there was a village named Vāsabha-gāma.
There, a resident monk named Kassapagotta was bound by his duties and made an effort, thinking:
"How might virtuous monks who have not yet come here come; how might those virtuous monks who have already come dwell in comfort; and how might this residence attain growth, increase, and expansion?
Now at that time, a number of monks, while wandering on tour among the Kāsis, arrived at the village of Vāsabha.
The monk Kassapagotta saw those monks coming from afar;
having seen them, he prepared seats, set out water for washing the feet, footstools, and foot-washing stones. He went out to meet them and received their bowls and robes.
He asked if they would like drinking water and made arrangements for a bath. He also made preparations for rice gruel, fresh food, and a meal.
Then it occurred to those visiting monks:
"This resident monk, friends, is indeed excellent; he makes an effort regarding bathing, and he also makes an effort regarding rice gruel, fresh food, and the meal.
Come then, friends, let us take up residence right here in Vāsabha Village."
Then those visiting monks took up residence right there in Vāsabhagāma.
Then it occurred to the monk of the Kassapa clan:
"The fatigue these visiting monks experienced upon their arrival has now subsided."
"These people were formerly ignorant of their proper sphere; now they are well-acquainted with their sphere.
It is indeed difficult to exert oneself for other families throughout one's entire life, and making requests is unpleasant to people.
What if I were no longer to exert myself regarding rice gruel, fresh food, and the meal?"
Thus, he did not make an effort regarding the rice gruel, the fresh foods, or the meal.
Then it occurred to those visiting monks:
"Formerly, friends, this resident monk made an effort regarding bathing; he even made an effort regarding the rice gruel, the fresh foods, and the meal."
“Now he does not even take the trouble to provide rice gruel, fresh food, or a meal.
This resident monk, friends, is wicked.
Come, friends, let us suspend this resident monk.”
Then those visiting monks gathered together and said this to the monk Kassapagotta:
“Formerly, friend, you were diligent regarding the bath; you were also diligent regarding the rice gruel, the fresh food, and the meal.
But now you are no longer diligent regarding the rice gruel, the fresh food, and the meal.”
“Friend, you have fallen into an offense.
Do you see that offense?
“Friend, I have no offense that I should see.”
Then those visiting monks suspended the monk Kassapagotta for not seeing an offense.
Then it occurred to the monk Kassapagotta:
"I do not know whether this is an offense or not an offense, whether I have committed it or not, or whether I have been suspended."
“I have not been suspended— whether by a legal or an illegal act, whether by a reversible or an irreversible act,
or whether by a formal act that is valid or one that is invalid.
What if I were to go to Campā and ask the Blessed One about this matter?”
Then the bhikkhu Kassapagotta, having put away his lodging and taking his bowl and robe, set out for Campā.
Traveling by stages, he approached Campā and went to where the Blessed One was. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhu Kassapagotta:
“Bhikkhu, I hope you are bearing up, I hope you are getting by;
I hope you have come along the road without too much fatigue?”
“And from where have you come, monk?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is livable, Blessed One.
And I have come along the road, Bhante, without much fatigue.”
“Venerable sir, there is a village named Vāsabha in the Kāsī country.
There, Blessed One, I am a resident, bound by my duties, and I have made an effort:

‘How might well-behaved bhikkhus who have not yet come here come; how might well-behaved bhikkhus who have already come dwell in comfort; and how might this residence attain growth, increase, and abundance?’”
Then, venerable sir, while wandering on tour among the Kāsīs, a number of bhikkhus arrived at Vāsabha village.
I saw those bhikkhus coming from afar, venerable sir;
having seen them, I prepared seats, set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-wiping cloth, and going out to meet them, I received their bowls and robes.
I asked for water, I made an effort regarding the bath, and I also made an effort regarding the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal.
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to those visiting monks:
"Friends, this resident monk is indeed excellent; he makes an effort regarding the bath, and he also makes an effort regarding the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal."
"Come then, friends, let us take up residence right here in Vāsabhagāma.
Then, Bhante, those visiting monks took up residence right there in Vāsabhagāma.
And it occurred to me, Bhante:
“The fatigue these visiting bhikkhus experienced upon their arrival has now subsided.
Those who were previously unskilled in seeking almsfood are now skilled in seeking it.
Furthermore, it is difficult to exert oneself for the sake of other families for as long as life lasts, and making requests of people is unpleasant.”
“What if I were not to make an effort regarding the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal?
Then, Bhante, I did not make an effort regarding the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal.
Then, Bhante, it occurred to those visiting monks:
“Formerly, friends, this resident monk used to take care regarding bathing; he also took care regarding rice porridge, fresh food, and the meal.
But now he does not take care regarding rice porridge, fresh food, or the meal.
This resident monk, friends, has become corrupted.”
"Come, friends, let us suspend the resident monk.
Then, venerable sir, those visiting monks gathered together and said this to me:
"Formerly, friend, you used to take great care regarding the bath, and you took great care regarding the rice gruel, the fresh food, and the meal."
“Now you do not take care regarding the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal.
Have you fallen into an offense, friend?
Do you see this offense?”
“‘Friends, there is no offense that I could see,’ I said.
Then, venerable sir, those visiting monks suspended me for not recognizing an offense.
Venerable sir, this thought occurred to me:”
‘Indeed, I do not know this: whether this is an offense or not an offense; whether I have committed it or not committed it; whether I have been suspended or not suspended;
whether [the act] was according to the Dhamma or not according to the Dhamma; whether it is reversible or irreversible;
whether it is a case that merits standing or does not merit standing.’
“What if I were to go to Campā and ask the Blessed One about this matter?
Then, Blessed One, I am coming from there.
“This, monk, is no offense; it is not an offense.”
You have not been suspended;
you are not suspended. You have not been ejected;
you are not ejected. You were ejected by an illegal act—one that is reversible and unfit for the occasion.
“Go, bhikkhu, and take up residence right there in Vāsabha village.
“Yes, Bhante,” the bhikkhu of the Kassapa clan replied to the Blessed One. He rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed for Vāsabha village.
Then those visiting bhikkhus felt remorse and experienced regret.
“It is a loss for us indeed, it is not a gain for us;
it is ill-gained by us indeed, it is not well-gained by us, that we have suspended a pure bhikkhu who was free from offense, without ground and without cause.
Come now, friends, let us go to Campā and confess our transgression as a transgression in the presence of the Blessed One.”
Then those visiting monks, having put away their lodgings and taking their bowls and robes, set out for Campā.
Traveling by stages, they approached Campā and went to where the Blessed One was. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting monks.
Then the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus:
“I hope you are bearing up, bhikkhus; I hope you are getting by;
I hope you have come along the road without too much fatigue?”
“And from where have you come, monks?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is livable, Blessed One.
And we have come along the road, Bhante, without much fatigue.”
“Venerable sir, there is a village called Vāsabha in the Kāsī country;
it is from there, Blessed One, that we have come.
“Bhikkhus, did you expel the resident bhikkhu?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In what basis, monks, on what grounds?
“It is without basis, Blessed One; it is without grounds.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unseemly, foolish men, it is unbecoming, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.
How can you, foolish men, suspend a pure bhikkhu who is without offense, on no ground and for no reason?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked them and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
‘Monks, a pure monk who is free from an offense must not be suspended without a basis and without cause.’”
"Whoever should suspend him, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Then those bhikkhus rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and said this to the Blessed One:

"We have transgressed, venerable sir; we have fallen into error as fools, as deluded, and as unskilled, in that we suspended a pure bhikkhu who was without offense, on a groundless and causeless basis."
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept our transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.
“Indeed, monks, you have committed a transgression—like those who are foolish, deluded, and unskilled—in that you suspended a pure monk who was without offense, on a groundless and causeless basis.
But since you, monks, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.”

They perform a factional legal act contrary to the Dhamma; they perform a united legal act contrary to the Dhamma;
they perform a factional legal act in accordance with the Dhamma; they perform a factional legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma;
they perform a united legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma.
One person suspends one person; one person suspends two people; one person suspends many people; one person suspends the Saṅgha.
Two people suspend one person; two people suspend two people; two people suspend many people; two people suspend the Saṅgha.
Many people suspend one person.
Many [monks] suspend two; many [monks] suspend many; many [monks] suspend a Saṅgha;
even a Saṅgha suspends a Saṅgha.
Those monks who are few in desires... [as before] ...they grumble, complain, and spread it about.
“How indeed can the monks in Campā perform such formal acts as these:
performing a factional act contrary to the Dhamma, performing a united act contrary to the Dhamma, performing a factional act in accordance with the Dhamma,
and performing a factional act that is a semblance of the Dhamma, or performing a united act that is a semblance of the Dhamma?”
They will act [thus]: one person will suspend another; one person will suspend two; one person will suspend many;
one person will suspend a Saṅgha; two people will suspend one; two people will suspend two;
two people will suspend many; two people will suspend a Saṅgha; and many people will suspend one.
“Many will suspend two; many will suspend many; many will suspend a Saṅgha;
and even a Saṅgha will suspend a Saṅgha.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that the monks in Campā perform such formal acts as these:
they perform a factional act contrary to the Dhamma … [and so on] … even the Saṅgha suspends another Saṅgha?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“Monks, it is unbecoming for those foolish men, it is unsuitable, it is unworthy, it is unbecoming of a recluse, it is improper, and it is not to be done.”
"How indeed, monks, can those foolish men perform such acts—performing a factional act contrary to the Dhamma... [and so on]...
even the Saṅgha shall suspend another Saṅgha?"
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:”
“Monks, if a factional legal act is performed contrary to the Dhamma, it is not a legal act and is not to be done;
if a united legal act is performed contrary to the Dhamma, it is not a legal act and is not to be done;
if a factional legal act is performed according to the Dhamma, it is not a legal act and is not to be done.”
A factional legal act performed by means of a semblance of the Dhamma is invalid and not to be carried out;
a united legal act performed by means of a semblance of the Dhamma is invalid and not to be carried out;
even a single person who suspends another is invalid and not to be carried out.
Even one person who suspends two [monks] performs an invalid act that is not to be done;
even one person who suspends many [monks] performs an invalid act that is not to be done;
even one person who suspends the Saṅgha performs an invalid act that is not to be done.
Even two [monks] who suspend one [monk] perform an invalid act that should not be done;
even two [monks] who suspend two [monks] perform an invalid act that should not be done;
even two [monks] who suspend a large number [of monks] perform an invalid act that should not be done.
Even two may suspend a Saṅgha; that is an invalid act and is not to be done.
Even many may suspend one; that is an invalid act and is not to be done.
Even many may suspend two; that is an invalid act and is not to be done.
Even a plurality suspends a plurality: it is not a legal act and is not to be done;
even a plurality suspends the Saṅgha: it is not a legal act and is not to be done;
even a Saṅgha suspends a Saṅgha: it is not a legal act and is not to be done.
“Monks, there are these four kinds of legal procedures:

a legal procedure that is contrary to the Dhamma and carried out by an incomplete assembly; a legal procedure that is contrary to the Dhamma but carried out by a complete assembly; a legal procedure that is in accordance with the Dhamma but carried out by an incomplete assembly;

and a legal procedure that is in accordance with the Dhamma and carried out by a complete assembly. In this regard, monks, that which is a legal procedure contrary to the Dhamma and carried out by an incomplete assembly—because it is contrary to the Dhamma and because it is carried out by an incomplete assembly—it is reversible and not fit to stand.”
“Monks, such a legal procedure is not to be performed, nor was such a procedure authorized by me.
In that regard, monks, as for this ‘unlawful procedure carried out by a unanimous assembly,’ monks, because it is unlawful, this procedure is reversible and unfit to stand.
Monks, such a procedure is not to be performed, nor was such a procedure authorized by me.”
In this regard, monks, that which is a factional legal act performed according to the Dhamma—this, monks, is a legal act that is reversible due to its factionality and is not fit for standing;
such an act, monks, should not be performed, nor was such an act authorized by me.

In this regard, monks, that which is a united legal act performed according to the Dhamma—this, monks, is a legal act that is irreversible due to its accordance with the Dhamma and its unity, and it is fit for standing.
“Monks, such a formal act (kamma) is to be performed; and such a formal act has been authorized by me.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall perform such a formal act as this—that is, one that is lawful and performed by a unanimous assembly.’”
3. Discussion on Formal Acts Deficient in Motion, etc.
Now at that time, the group of six monks performed such formal acts as these:
they performed a formal act contrary to the Dhamma by a divided assembly; they performed a formal act contrary to the Dhamma by a united assembly.
They perform a factional legal act in accordance with the Dhamma; they perform a factional legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma;

they perform a united legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma; they perform a legal act that is deficient in the motion but complete in the proclamation; they perform a legal act that is deficient in the proclamation but complete in the motion; they perform a legal act that is deficient both in the motion and in the proclamation;
they perform a legal act apart from the Dhamma; they perform a legal act apart from the Vinaya; they perform a legal act apart from the Teacher’s instruction.
They perform even those formal acts that are censurable, contrary to the Dhamma, reversible, and unfit to stand.
Those monks who have few desires... [and so on]... they complain, criticize, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group of six monks perform such formal acts as these?"
They will perform a factional legal act contrary to the Dhamma; they will perform a united legal act contrary to the Dhamma;

they will perform a factional legal act according to the Dhamma; they will perform a factional legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma; they will perform a united legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma;

they will perform a legal act that is deficient in the motion but complete in the proclamation; they will perform a legal act that is deficient in the proclamation but complete in the motion; and they will perform a legal act that is deficient both in the motion and in the proclamation.
“They will perform legal procedures contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Teacher’s instruction;
they will even perform legal procedures that are censured, non-Dhammic, reversible, and unfit to stand.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks perform such formal acts as these:
they perform a factional act contrary to the Dhamma … [and so on] … they even perform a censurable act that is contrary to the Dhamma, reversible, and unfit for its purpose?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One,
rebuked him … having rebuked him and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, if an action is performed contrary to the Dhamma by a faction, it is not a valid legal act and should not be done;
if an action is performed contrary to the Dhamma by a unanimous assembly, it is not a valid legal act and should not be done;
if an action is performed according to the Dhamma by a faction, it is not a valid legal act and should not be done.”
An action performed by a faction that is a semblance of Dhamma is invalid and not to be done;
an action performed by a unanimous assembly that is a semblance of Dhamma is invalid and not to be done.
Monks, if an action is deficient in the motion but complete in the proclamation, it is invalid and not to be done.
“Monks, if a legal procedure is deficient in its proclamation but complete in its motion, it is not a valid act and is not to be performed.
If a legal procedure is deficient in its motion but deficient in its proclamation, it is not a valid act and is not to be performed.
Furthermore, if a legal procedure is contrary to the Dhamma, it is not a valid act and is not to be performed.”
Even if it is apart from the discipline (*vinaya*), an act is invalid and should not be performed;
even if it is apart from the Teacher’s instruction (*satthusāsana*), an act is invalid and should not be performed.
If an act has been done in a way that is censured, monks, it is contrary to the Dhamma, reversible, unfit for standing, invalid, and should not be performed.
“Monks, there are these five kinds of legal procedures:

an illegal procedure, a factional procedure, a united procedure, a factional procedure that is a semblance of the Dharma, and a united procedure that is a semblance of the Dharma; and, monks, a united procedure that is in accordance with the Dharma.
And what, monks, is an illegal procedure?”

If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), one performs the act with only the motion and does not proclaim the formal statement (*kammavācā*), it is an illegitimate act.
If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and one proclamation, one performs the act with two motions and does not proclaim the formal statement, it is an illegitimate act.
If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and one proclamation, one performs the act with only one proclamation and does not establish the motion, it is an illegitimate act.
Monks, if in a formal act requiring a motion and a second proclamation, one performs the act with two proclamations but does not put forward the motion, it is an illegitimate act. Monks,
if in a formal act requiring a motion and a fourth proclamation, one performs the act with only one motion but does not announce the proclamations,
it is an illegitimate act.

"Monks, if in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), one performs the act with two motions and does not proclaim the formal statement (*kammavācā*), it is an illegitimate act.
Monks, if in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, one performs the act with three motions and does not proclaim the formal statement, it is an illegitimate act.
Monks, if in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, one performs the act with four motions and does not proclaim the formal statement, it is an illegitimate act."

Monks, if in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), one performs the act with only one proclamation and does not establish the motion, it is an illegitimate act (*adhammakamma*).
Monks, if in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, one performs the act with two proclamations and does not establish the motion, it is an illegitimate act.
Monks, if in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, one performs the act with three proclamations and does not establish the motion, it is an illegitimate act.
If, monks, in a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation, one performs the act with four proclamations but does not establish the motion—it is an illegitimate act.
This, monks, is called an illegitimate act.
And what, monks, is a factional act?

If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), as many monks as are entitled to participate in the act have not arrived, the consent of those entitled to give it has not been brought, and those present raise an objection—it is a factional act.

If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and one proclamation, as many monks as are entitled to participate in the act have arrived, but the consent of those entitled to give it has not been brought, and those present raise an objection—it is a factional act.

If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and a second, as many monks as are entitled to participate have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forward, yet those present raise an objection—it is a factional act.

If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and a fourth [announcement], as many monks as are entitled to participate have not arrived, the consent of those entitled to give their consent has not been brought forward, yet those present raise an objection—it is a factional act.

If, monks, in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), as many monks as are entitled to participate have arrived, but the consent of those who ought to give their consent has not been brought, and those present raise an objection—it is a factional act (*vaggakamma*).

If, monks, in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, as many monks as are entitled to participate have arrived, and the consent of those who ought to give their consent has been brought, but those present raise an objection—it is a factional act.
This, monks, is called a factional act.
And what, monks, is a legal act performed by a unanimous assembly?

If, monks, in a legal act requiring a motion and a second, as many monks as are entitled to participate have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forth, and those present do not protest—it is a legal act performed by a unanimous assembly.

If, monks, in a legal act requiring a motion and a fourth [announcement], as many monks as are entitled to participate have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forth, and those present do not protest—it is a legal act performed by a unanimous assembly.
This, monks, is called a legal act performed by a united assembly.
And what, monks, is a factional legal act that is a mere semblance of the Dhamma?
If, monks, in a legal act requiring a motion and a second [announcement], one proclaims the formal statement first and places the motion afterwards—
When as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have not arrived, when the consent of those who ought to give their consent has not been brought,
and when those present raise an objection— this is a factional act that is a mere semblance of the Dhamma.
If, in a formal act requiring a motion and one proclamation, one proclaims the formal statement first and puts forward the motion afterwards...
When as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have arrived, but the consent of those who are required to give their consent has not been brought,
and those present raise an objection— this is a factional act that is a mere semblance of the Dhamma.

If, in a formal act requiring a motion and one proclamation, he first recites the formal statement and afterwards puts forward the motion— this is a factional act that is a mere semblance of the Dhamma.
When as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought,
and they are present before the assembly, yet they protest— a formal act performed by a faction using a semblance of the Dhamma.
If, monks, in a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, one proclaims the formal words first and the motion afterwards...
It is set aside when: those monks who are entitled to participate in the legal act have not arrived; the consent of those who are required to give their consent has not been brought;
and those present raise an objection. This is a factional legal act that is a mere semblance of Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, if in a legal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, one proclaims the formal statement first and the motion afterwards...
It is set aside when: the monks who are entitled to participate in the legal act have arrived; the consent of those entitled to give their consent has not been brought forward;
and those present raise an objection. This is a factional legal act that is a mere semblance of the Dhamma.
Monks, if in a legal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, one proclaims the formal statement first and the motion afterwards...
He sets it aside; the monks who are entitled to perform the legal act have arrived; the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought;
yet those present raise an objection. This is a factional legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma.
This, monks, is called a factional legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma.
And what, monks, is a united legal act that is a counterfeit of the Dhamma?
If, monks, in a legal act requiring a motion and a second proclamation, one proclaims the formal statement first and places the motion afterwards;

and if as many monks as are entitled to participate in the act have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forth, and they are present in person—this is a united legal act that is a counterfeit of the Dhamma.
They do not protest against a united legal act that is a mere semblance of Dhamma.
Monks, if in a legal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations, he first proclaims the formal act (*kammavācā*) and afterwards puts forward the motion,
and as many monks as are entitled to participate in the act have arrived, and the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought— [then it is invalid].
They are present and do not protest; this is a united legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma.
This, monks, is called a united legal act that is a semblance of the Dhamma.
And what, monks, is a united legal act that is in accordance with the Dhamma?
If, monks, in a formal act requiring a motion and a second, one first puts forward the motion and afterwards performs the formal act with a single proclamation,
and as many monks as are entitled to participate have arrived, the consent of those who ought to give it has been brought forth,
and those present do not protest— it is a legitimate formal act performed by a unanimous assembly.
If, monks, in a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation, one first puts forward the motion and afterwards performs the act with three proclamations;
and if as many monks as are entitled to participate in the act have arrived, the consent of those who are entitled to give it has been brought forth,
and those present do not protest— it is a legitimate act performed by a unanimous assembly.
This, monks, is called a legal act performed by a unanimous assembly.

7. Discussion on Unlawful Acts, etc.
Now, monks, there may be a case where a monk has no offense that needs to be seen.
The Saṅgha, or several monks, or a single individual, exhorts him:
“Friend, you have fallen into an offense; do you see this offense?
He speaks thus:
‘Friends, I have no offense that I could see.
If the Saṅgha suspends him for not seeing an offense,
it is an illegitimate legal procedure.
But here, monks, a monk has no offense to be confessed.
Yet the Saṅgha, or several individuals, or a single person, accuses him, saying:
“Friend, you have fallen into an offense; confess that offense.”
Thus he speaks:
“Friends, I have no offense that I should make amends for.
The Saṅgha suspends him for not making amends for an offense.
This is an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*).
Furthermore, monks, when a monk does not relinquish an evil view,

“Friend, your view is evil; relinquish this evil view.
He says this:
“Friends, I have no evil view that I should relinquish.”
If the Saṅgha suspends him for not relinquishing a pernicious view,
that is an illegitimate legal act.
Furthermore, monks, there may be a case where for a monk there is no offense to be seen, nor any offense to be atoned for.

“Friend, you have fallen into an offense; do you see this offense?

“Friend, you have fallen into an offense; do you see this offense?

If the Saṅgha suspends him for not seeing [an offense], or for not making amends for it, or for not relinquishing [a wrong view]—

But in this case, monks, there is an offense of a monk that ought to be seen.
The Saṅgha, or several monks, or a single individual, urges him:
“Friend, you have fallen into an offense; do you see this offense?
He replies thus:
‘Friends, I have no offense that I could see.
If the Sangha suspends him for not seeing an offense,
it is a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma).
But here, monks, a monk has an offense that must be confessed.
The Saṅgha, or several individuals, or a single person, accuses him, saying:
"Friend, you have committed an offense; confess that offense."
Thus he speaks:
“Friends, I have no offense that I should make amends for.
The Sangha suspends him for not making amends for an offense.
This is a legal act in accordance with the Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk has a wicked view that ought to be relinquished,
the Saṅgha, or several individuals, or a single person, may admonish him:
“‘Friend, your view is evil; relinquish this evil view.
He says:
‘Friends, I have no evil view that I should relinquish.’”
The Saṅgha suspends him for not relinquishing a pernicious view—
this is a legal act in accordance with the Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, there is the case where a monk has an offense that must be seen, and there is an offense that must be confessed … [as before] …”
There is an offense that must be recognized; there is an evil view that must be relinquished … [as before] … There is an offense that must be confessed;

there is an evil view that must be relinquished … [as before] … There is an offense that must be recognized, there is an offense that must be confessed, and there is an evil view that must be relinquished.
The Saṅgha, or several monks, or a single individual, should exhort him thus:
“Friend, you have fallen into an offense; do you see this offense?
Make amends for that offense.”
“Your view is evil; relinquish this evil view.
He says this:
“Friends, I have no offense that I should see.”
‘Friends, I have no offense that I should make amends for;
friends, I have no evil view that I should relinquish.
The Sangha then suspends him for failure to acknowledge [an offense], or for failure to make amends, or for failure to relinquish [an evil view].
“...a legal act according to the Dhamma. 8.
The Discourse on Upāli’s Questions:
Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, if a Saṅgha that is complete performs a legal procedure that ought to be performed in the presence [of the accused] without being in their presence, is that a legal procedure, venerable sir, and a procedure in accordance with the Vinaya?
“That, Upāli, is an illegal procedure and not a procedure in accordance with the Vinaya.”

“Venerable sir, when a united Saṅgha performs a legal procedure that requires interrogation without interrogation … performs a legal procedure that requires admission without admission … grants the verdict of non-delusion to one who deserves the verdict of mindfulness …”
They perform a *tassapāpiyasika* legal procedure against one who deserves a *amūḷhavinaya*;
they perform a *tajjanīya* legal procedure against one who deserves a *tassapāpiyasika*;
they perform a *niyassa* legal procedure against one who deserves a *tajjanīya*.
They perform an act of banishment against one who deserves an act of demotion;
they perform an act of reconciliation against one who deserves an act of banishment;
they perform an act of suspension against one who deserves an act of reconciliation.
He grants probation to one who deserves the act of suspension;
he sends back to the beginning one who deserves probation;
he grants the trial period to one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning.

“If one rehabilitates one who deserves the *mānatta* penance… or confers full ordination on one who deserves rehabilitation, is that, Bhante, a legal act according to the Dhamma, or a legal act according to the Vinaya?
“That, Upāli, is an illegal act; it is not a legal act according to the Vinaya.”

Upāli, when a united Saṅgha performs a formal act that requires to be done in the presence [of the accused] in his absence, this, Upāli, is an illegal act and an act not in accordance with the Vinaya; and thus the Saṅgha is at fault.

Upāli, when a united Saṅgha performs a formal act that requires to be done after interrogation without interrogation … [and so on] … performs a formal act that requires to be done by confession without confession … [and so on] … [it is an illegal act and an act not in accordance with the Vinaya; and thus the Saṅgha is at fault].
He grants a verdict of past insanity to one who deserves a verdict of past insanity;
he carries out a legal procedure of further penalty against one who deserves a verdict of past insanity;
he carries out a censure transaction against one who deserves a legal procedure of further penalty.
They carry out a demotion against one deserving of a censure;
they carry out an exile against one deserving of a demotion;
they carry out a reconciliation against one deserving of an exile.
He performs a formal act of suspension against one who deserves a formal act of reconciliation;
he grants probation to one who deserves a formal act of suspension;
he sends back to the beginning one who deserves probation.
If one grants the *mānatta* penance to one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning;
if one rehabilitates one who deserves the *mānatta*;
or if one confers full ordination on one who deserves rehabilitation—in this way, Upāli, it is an illegal act and an act not in accordance with the discipline.
“And furthermore, the Saṅgha would be acting in excess of its authority.
“Venerable sir, if a unanimous Saṅgha performs a formal act that ought to be performed in the presence [of the accused] in their presence, is that a legal act, venerable sir, and a disciplinary act?
“That is a legal act, Upāli, and a disciplinary act.”
“Venerable sir, when a united Saṅgha performs a legal procedure that requires interrogation by means of interrogation...
performs a legal procedure that requires admission by means of admission...
grants the resolution through recollection to one who deserves the resolution through recollection...”
He grants the verdict of past insanity to one deserving of the verdict of past insanity;
he carries out the legal procedure of further penalty against one deserving of the legal procedure of further penalty;
he carries out the legal procedure of censure against one deserving of the legal procedure of censure.
They perform a *niyassakamma* against one who deserves a *niyassakamma*;
they perform a *pabbājanīyakamma* against one who deserves a *pabbājanīyakamma*;
they perform a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* against one who deserves a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma*.
He performs an act of suspension against one who deserves an act of suspension;
he grants probation to one who deserves probation;
he sends back to the beginning one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning.
"If one grants the *mānatta* penance to one who deserves it;
rehabilitates one who deserves rehabilitation;
or confers full ordination on one who deserves it—is that, venerable sir, a legal act according to the Dhamma, a legal act according to the Vinaya?"
“Upāli, that is a legal act; it is a disciplinary act.

Upāli, when a united Saṅgha performs a formal act that requires being performed in the presence [of those concerned] in their very presence, in this way, Upāli, it is a legal act and a disciplinary act.
And in this way, the Saṅgha is not at fault.”
Upāli, when a united Saṅgha performs a formal act that requires interrogation by means of interrogation;
when it performs a formal act that requires admission by means of admission;
or when it grants the resolution through recollection to one who deserves the resolution through recollection—[this is a legitimate procedure].
He grants the verdict of past insanity to one deserving of the verdict of past insanity;
he carries out the legal procedure of further penalty against one deserving of the legal procedure of further penalty;
he carries out the legal procedure of censure against one deserving of the legal procedure of censure.
They perform a *niyassakamma* against one who deserves a *niyassakamma*;
they perform a *pabbājanīyakamma* against one who deserves a *pabbājanīyakamma*;
they perform a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* against one who deserves a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma*.
He performs an act of suspension against one who deserves an act of suspension;
he grants probation to one who deserves probation;
he sends back to the beginning one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning.
If one grants the *mānatta* penance to one who deserves the *mānatta* penance;
if one rehabilitates one who deserves rehabilitation;
if one confers full ordination on one who deserves full ordination—in this way, Upāli, there is a legal act that is in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
"And in this way, the Saṅgha remains free from transgression.

"Venerable sir, if a unanimous Saṅgha grants a verdict of past insanity to one who deserves a verdict of mindfulness, or grants a verdict of mindfulness to one who deserves a verdict of past insanity, is that a legal act according to the Dhamma, venerable sir, or is it a legal act according to the Vinaya?
"Upāli, that is an illegal act; it is not a legal act according to the Vinaya."
“Venerable sir, if a united Saṅgha performs a *tassapāpiyasika* (further-punishment) legal act against one who deserves *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity),
or grants *amūḷhavinaya* to one who deserves a *tassapāpiyasika* legal act … [and so on] … or performs a *tajjanīya* (reproof) legal act against one who deserves a *tassapāpiyasika* legal act,

or performs a *tassapāpiyasika* legal act against one who deserves a *tajjanīya* legal act … or performs a *niyassa* (banishment) legal act against one who deserves a *tajjanīya* legal act, or performs a *tajjanīya* legal act against one who deserves a *niyassa* legal act …”
They perform an act of banishment against one deserving an act of demotion; they perform an act of demotion against one deserving an act of banishment...
they perform an act of reconciliation against one deserving an act of banishment; they perform an act of banishment against one deserving an act of reconciliation...
they perform an act of suspension against one deserving an act of reconciliation; they perform an act of reconciliation against one deserving an act of suspension...

He grants probation to one who deserves a formal act of suspension; he performs a formal act of suspension against one who deserves probation… he sends back to the beginning one who deserves probation;

he grants probation to one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning… he grants the trial period (mānatta) to one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning; he sends back to the beginning one who deserves the trial period…
“He grants rehabilitation to one who deserves the trial period;

he grants the trial period to one who deserves rehabilitation… he confers full ordination on one who deserves rehabilitation; he rehabilitates one who deserves full ordination. Venerable sir, is that a legal act (dhammakamma) or a disciplinary act (vinayakamma)?
“Upāli, that is an illegal act (adhammakamma), it is not a disciplinary act.”

Upāli, when a unanimous Saṅgha grants a verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*) to one who deserves a verdict of mindfulness (*sativinaya*), or grants a verdict of mindfulness to one who deserves a verdict of past insanity—in this way, Upāli, it is an illegal act and a non-disciplinary act;
furthermore, the Saṅgha has overstepped its bounds.

Upāli, when a unanimous Saṅgha performs a legal procedure of further penalty (*tassapāpiyasikākamma*) against one who deserves a verdict of past insanity, or grants a verdict of past insanity to one who deserves a legal procedure of further penalty … [and so forth].
They perform a *tajjanīya-kamma* against one who deserves a *tassapāpiyasika-kamma*; they perform a *tassapāpiyasika-kamma* against one who deserves a *tajjanīya-kamma*.
They perform a *niyassakamma* against one who deserves a *tajjanīya-kamma*; they perform a *tajjanīya-kamma* against one who deserves a *niyassakamma*.
They perform a *pabbājanīya-kamma* against one who deserves a *niyassakamma*; they perform a *niyassakamma* against one who deserves a *pabbājanīya-kamma*.
He performs a procedure of reconciliation against one deserving a procedure of banishment; he performs a procedure of banishment against one deserving a procedure of reconciliation...
he performs a procedure of suspension against one deserving a procedure of reconciliation; he performs a procedure of reconciliation against one deserving a procedure of suspension...
he grants probation to one deserving a procedure of suspension; he performs a procedure of suspension against one deserving probation...
He sends back to the beginning one who deserves probation; he grants probation to one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning;
he grants the trial period (mānatta) to one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning; he sends back to the beginning one who deserves the trial period;
he rehabilitates one who deserves the trial period; he grants the trial period to one who deserves rehabilitation.

“If one grants full ordination to someone who deserves rehabilitation, or rehabilitates someone who deserves full ordination—in this way, Upāli, it is an illegitimate legal act and a non-disciplinary act.
Furthermore, in doing so, the Saṅgha oversteps its authority.

“Venerable sir, if a unanimous Saṅgha grants the verdict of mindfully remembered to one who deserves the verdict of mindfully remembered, or grants the verdict of past insanity to one who deserves the verdict of past insanity—is that, venerable sir, a legitimate legal act and a disciplinary act?”
“Upāli, that is a legal act of the Dhamma; it is a legal act of the Vinaya.
“But, Bhante, when a concordant Saṅgha grants the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) to one who deserves the *amūḷhavinaya*...
[and so on] ...when it performs the *tassapāpiyasikākamma* (act of further penalty) against one who deserves the *tassapāpiyasikākamma*... [and so on] ...
They perform a censure act against one who deserves a censure act; ...
they perform a demotion act against one who deserves a demotion act; ...
they perform an banishment act against one who deserves a banishment act; ... [and so on].
He performs an act of reconciliation against one deserving of an act of reconciliation...
he performs an act of suspension against one deserving of an act of suspension...
he grants probation to one deserving of probation... [and so forth].
"If one sends back to the beginning one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning...
[and so on] ...if one grants the trial period (mānatta) to one who deserves the trial period...

[and so on] ...if one rehabilitates one who deserves rehabilitation, or if one confers full ordination (upasampadā) upon one who deserves full ordination—Venerable Sir, is that a legal act according to the Dhamma, a legal act according to the Vinaya?"
“Upāli, that is a legal act (*dhammakamma*), it is a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*).

Upāli, when a united Saṅgha grants the verdict of mindfulness to one deserving of the verdict of mindfulness, and grants the verdict of past insanity to one deserving of the verdict of past insanity—in this way, Upāli, it is a legal act and a disciplinary act.
And in this way, the Saṅgha does not overstep its authority.”
Upāli, when a harmonious Saṅgha grants the verdict of "not being insane" to one who deserves the verdict of "not being insane," ... [and so on] ...
performs the legal act of "further penalty" against one who deserves the legal act of "further penalty," ... [and so on] ...
performs the legal act of "reproof" against one who deserves the legal act of "reproof," ... [and so on].
They perform a *niyassakamma* against one who deserves a *niyassakamma*; ...
they perform a *pabbājanīyakamma* against one who deserves a *pabbājanīyakamma*; ...
they perform a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* against one who deserves a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma*; ... [and so on].
He performs an act of suspension against one who deserves an act of suspension; ...
he grants probation to one who deserves probation; ...
he sends back to the beginning one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning; ... [and so forth].
“He grants the *mānatta* penance to one who deserves the *mānatta* penance...

[and so on] ...he rehabilitates one who deserves rehabilitation, he ordains one who deserves ordination. In this way, Upāli, it is a legal act according to the Dhamma and a legal act according to the Vinaya;
and thus the Saṅgha is not at fault.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, when a united Saṅgha grants a verdict of past insanity to one who deserves a verdict of mindfulness, that, bhikkhus, is an illegal act and a non-disciplinary act.
And in this way, the Saṅgha has overstepped its bounds.”
“Monks, when a united Saṅgha performs a *tassapāpiyasika* legal procedure against one who deserves *sativinaya*; ...
performs a *tajjanīya* legal procedure against one who deserves *sativinaya*; ...
performs a *niyassa* legal procedure against one who deserves *sativinaya*...”
They carry out a procedure of banishment against one deserving of settlement through recollection;
they carry out a procedure of reconciliation against one deserving of settlement through recollection;
they carry out a procedure of suspension against one deserving of settlement through recollection.
He grants probation to one who deserves resolution through recollection;
he sends back to the beginning one who deserves resolution through recollection;
he grants the trial period (mānatta) to one who deserves resolution through recollection.
If one grants a verdict of past insanity to one who deserves a verdict of past insanity,
or if one confers full ordination upon one who deserves a verdict of past insanity— in this way, monks, it is an illegal act, a non-disciplinary act;
and thus the Saṅgha acts with transgression.
“Monks, when a united Saṅgha carries out a *tassapāpiyasika-kamma* against one who deserves *amūḷhavinaya*, that is an illegitimate legal act, a non-disciplinary act;
and thus the Saṅgha acts in excess of its authority.
When a united Saṅgha carries out a *tajjanīya-kamma* against one who deserves *amūḷhavinaya* … [and so on] …”
They carry out a formal act of demotion against one who deserves resolution through past insanity;
they carry out a formal act of banishment against one who deserves resolution through past insanity;
they carry out a formal act of reconciliation against one who deserves resolution through past insanity.
He carries out a formal act of suspension against one who deserves resolution through past insanity;
he grants probation to one who deserves resolution through past insanity;
he sends back to the beginning one who deserves resolution through past insanity.
He grants the trial period (mānatta) to one deserving of resolution through past insanity;
he rehabilitates one deserving of resolution through past insanity;
he ordains one deserving of resolution through past insanity.
If a Saṅgha grants the verdict of mindfulness to one who deserves the verdict of not being insane, this, monks, is an illegal act and a non-disciplinary act;
furthermore, the Saṅgha acts in excess of its authority.
If a unanimous Saṅgha performs a censure-act against one who deserves the act of further penalty... [and so on].
one deserving of a censure act … one deserving of a demotion act … one deserving of a banishment act …
one deserving of a procedure of reconciliation … one deserving of a procedure of suspension … one deserving of probation …
one deserving to be sent back to the beginning … one deserving the period of trial (mānatta) … one deserving rehabilitation (abbhāna) …
If one grants a verdict of mindfulness (*sativinaya*) to someone who is eligible for full ordination (*upasampadāraha*), in this way, monks, it is an illegal act and a non-disciplinary act;
furthermore, the Saṅgha thereby acts in transgression.
If, monks, a unanimous Saṅgha grants a verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*) to someone who is eligible for full ordination... [and so on].
He performs a *tassapāpiyasikā* (further-punishment) legal act against one who is eligible for full ordination;
he performs a *tajjanīya* (reproval) legal act against one who is eligible for full ordination;
he performs a *niyassakamma* (demotion) legal act against one who is eligible for full ordination.
He carries out a formal act of banishment against one who is eligible for full ordination;
he carries out a formal act of reconciliation against one who is eligible for full ordination;
he carries out a formal act of suspension against one who is eligible for full ordination.
He grants probation to one who is eligible for full ordination;
he sends back to the beginning one who is eligible for full ordination;
he grants the period of penance (mānatta) to one who is eligible for full ordination.
“If one grants full ordination to one who is worthy of it, in this way, monks, there is an illegal act and an act not in accordance with the discipline.
Furthermore, the Saṅgha has overstepped its bounds.
The second section of recitation, consisting of Upāli’s questions, is finished.
